newsitem.title: SPAIN: Club Med spread over Bunds seen declining steadily.
newsitem.headline: Club Med spread over Bunds seen declining steadily.

text.p: Europe's "Club Med" countries have dramatically slimmed down their 10-year bond spreads to Bunds in recent months, but analysts said they have not yet achieved an ideal shape.

After their last moves, a pause would be likely in coming weeks, analysts said. But they said longer-term forcasts hinted at further declines in spreads, especially if markets believe in the groups' timely entry into Europe's single currency.

"Right now, the 10-year (Spanish) bonos-Bunds spread is likely to stop where it is, but I would not be surprised if it were to go down further to 135/140 basis points," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

On Thursday, the 10-year spread between bonos and German Bunds reached a record low, narrowing as far as 145 basis points. It has contracted from 330 basis points at the start of March or from 500 in the summer of 1995.
Salomon Brother's economist Jose Luis Alzola expected this differential to narrow to 100 basis points in a year's time.
Another analyst said "My target was at 150 basis points. But now, I guess the next one is around 100 by the end of the first quarter in 1997 if the tone of the market continues positive."

Cesar Molinas, of Merrill Lynch in Madrid, said further reductions would not occur "unless markets price in early EMU entry, which is something, which despite all this euro-optimism, markets haven't yet started to do."
But optimists said peripheral markets will be strong if they continue to draw strength from U.S. Treasury bonds.

"Bonos and (Italian) Btps are positive because of good news on EMU convergence, but this bullishness came also from the U.S. market. As it will continue to rise, our markets will rise as well," said Lumholdt.
Looking at the Club Med group, economists said they preferred the "tinier bits." They are rating Portugal over Spain, and Spain over Italy when judging their chances of joining the euro's launch.

The Italian spread over Bunds, which declined to 179 basis points from more than 410 in March 1996 and from more than 500 basis points in the summer of 1995, is expected to shrink toward 150-160 basis points in coming weeks, analysts said.

Portugal's prospects are even better. The 10-year spread is now trading about 137 basis points over Bunds and could fall to 120 basis points by year end and to 90 basis points in a year, said Mario Vigario, head of trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.

He said Portugal's chances to be in the launch are higher than Spain's from an economic point of view. He forecast the 10-year spread over Bonos, now trading at 12 basis points under, would expand toward 25 basis points by year-end and toward 40 basis points in 12 months.

"But from a political point of view, it's different. And this is what the market is discounting -- the fact that Spain and Italy will enter together," Lumholdt said, explaining why the spread between Italian btps and Spanish bonos declined from 90 basis points in September to 30 basis points.
But he added this value should stabilize. "Italy is a riskier investment. I'd be long on Spain and short on Italy."
